 She Bought a $482,000 Arizona Snowbird Home and Planned to Stay Seven Months. Medicare Advantage May Drop Her Plan Before She Returns
 A seven-month Arizona winter felt like a reasonable plan until her Medicare Advantage coverage started a clock she never knew existed. One month over the limit can unravel the coverage she paid into all year.
 By Gerelyn Terzo 
 Published October 25, 2026, 12:00pm ET · 4 min read 
 The Full Benefits Desk desk. Editor: Gerelyn Terzo .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Medicare Advantage plans must drop members who stay outside their service area for more than 6 consecutive months, even without a permanent move.
 Some plans offer a visitor/traveler benefit extending the limit to 12 months, but coverage varies by plan and destination state.
 If disenrolled, Original Medicare applies nationwide but has no out-of-pocket cap and 2026 hospital deductibles reach $1,736 per benefit period.

 Imagine a retiree who just closed on a $482,000 winter home in Arizona. She plans to spend seven months there, then fly home. She kept her house up north, her doctors up north and her Medicare Advantage plan up north. Her plan is a preferred provider organization (PPO), with coverage for out-of-network care. Between that flexibility and the house she still owns, she figures she’s covered.
 Keeping the house doesn’t guarantee she can keep the plan. Medicare Advantage has rules for both permanent moves and extended trips away from home. Without a qualifying traveler benefit, seven consecutive months in Arizona can cost her the coverage she kept up north. Retirees enrolled in Original Medicare can see any provider in the country that accepts Medicare. Original Medicare won’t put a six-month limit on her winter stay.
 Medicare Advantage Has a Service-Area Clock
 Each Medicare Advantage plan has a defined service area, usually a group of counties. Federal rules generally require the plan to drop a member who stays outside that area for more than 6 consecutive months, even if she hasn’t permanently moved.
 That’s the catch. She can still consider the northern house her home and lose her plan because she stayed away too long. Without an exception, her seven-month season puts her coverage at risk before her flight home.
 Some Plans Give Snowbirds More Time
 A visitor/traveler benefit can buy her more time. Some plans allow members to stay elsewhere in the United States for up to 12 consecutive months, but others set a shorter limit. If her plan allows the full year, disenrollment takes effect on the first day of the 13th month. She needs her plan’s deadline before choosing her return date.
 Plans decide whether to offer the benefit, and those that do can limit it to certain parts of the country. Her plan could cover visitors in Florida and skip Arizona entirely. A PPO’s out-of-network coverage is a separate feature: paying out-of-network claims leaves the service-area clock running. Her Evidence of Coverage, the long document plans send each fall, states whether a visitor/traveler benefit exists and where it applies. She should read it before she books the season.
 Losing the Plan Opens a New Election Window
 If the plan disenrolls her for being out of the area, she gets a special election period to pick new coverage, such as another Advantage plan or Original Medicare combined with a standalone Part D drug plan . If she lets that window close without choosing, Medicare treats her as having elected Original Medicare, which can leave her without drug coverage until she signs up for Part D.
 Original Medicare works in Arizona and back home with any provider that accepts Medicare, but it comes with real cost exposure. In 2026 she faces a $283 Part B deductible, a $1,736 Part A hospital deductible per benefit period, and hospital coinsurance of $434 per day for days 61 through 90, with no annual out-of-pocket ceiling. A Medigap policy can cover many of those bills, depending on the policy. It doesn’t automatically cover every deductible or copayment.
 She should also check whether losing her Advantage plan gives her a protected opportunity to buy Medigap without being rejected or charged more because of her health. Moving out of a plan’s service area can create that right. For her extended winter stay, she should have her State Health Insurance Assistance Program review the disenrollment notice and confirm which protections and deadlines apply.
 Count the Months Before Crossing State Lines
 Before leaving, contact the plan. Report the dates of the absence and ask two questions: Does the plan offer a visitor/traveler benefit, and does it cover Arizona?
 Confirm providers in both places. Line up primary care, urgent care and a pharmacy in Arizona that her plan will pay for, and make sure her doctors back home stay in network for her return.
 Fit the calendar to the rules. For a temporary stay without a traveler benefit, keep the absence to 6 consecutive months or less. With a traveler benefit, return within the time her plan allows. Ask for that deadline in writing.
 Watch the mailbox as well. When the plan knows about her absence, the notice generally comes within the first 10 calendar days of month six, or the final permitted month under a traveler benefit. If the plan learns about the trip after she has already overstayed, a different notice deadline applies. She should call as soon as a letter arrives, but silence from the plan isn’t permission to stay longer.
 Open Enrollment Is the Moment to Fix This
 Medicare’s annual open enrollment runs through December 7, with changes taking effect January 1. A snowbird comparing plans for next year should put the visitor/traveler benefit on her checklist right next to premiums, drug lists and networks (we mapped out the surcharges and coverage gaps that trip up retirees at this stage in a free Medicare guide ). A lower premium can lose its appeal quickly if the plan can’t keep her covered through the winter.
 She bought the Arizona house for the freedom to stay longer. Before settling in for seven months, she needs to know whether her Medicare plan can stay with her.
